But time moves differently on Love Island Australia , where a select few leave " the outside world " behind . <p> Competently captained by Sophie Monk , with delightfully unhinged voiceovers by comedian Eoghan McDermott , the dating reality show focuses on a group of contestants in their 20s ( " islanders " ) living in an eminently Instagrammable Spanish villa . They are continuously monitored while trying @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " ) to avoid being dumped from the cast and , ultimately , to find true love and win a cash prize . <p> Season six starts with 10 contestants . After a rigorous make-out session to " try before they buy " , the five men ( Kane , Zane , Indigo , Niko and Dylan ) and five women ( Em , Eilisha , Hannah , Mimi and Xanthe ) pair off . Aside from the fact that her " Prince Charming moment " had been with Zane , Hannah and Niko seem besotted . Later , they have their first kiss during a game of spin the bottle . <p> " I manifested that last spin , " Niko casually informed Hannah on the lush patio . <p> " Are you just saying that ' cause you knew I manifested this ? ' " Hannah inquired . " Or are you a manifester ? " <p> But they picnic , as Auden once put it , on the edge of a precipice . Over 29 hour-long episodes , the contestants -- as well as the Australian public @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vote to decide who stays in the villa and , eventually , which couple wins . Adding to this capriciousness , new contestants ( " bombshells " ) can be dropped into the mix at any time to shake things up . Like tatted Taylor , 28 , who strides into that heteronormative Narnia and receives the " #WelcomeGift " of selecting two women for a kiss . <p> One of them was Hannah . Her ensuing delight rattled Niko , prompting him to pull " his girl " aside for their alfresco chat , where cracks surfaced before being quickly concealed in the name of love , or strategy . But perhaps not for long . While Taylor forgets what language one of his tattoos is in , the memory of Hannah 's kiss and their agreeable banter over the relative merits of scrotox could very well linger . <p> Producers of competitive dating shows have grown increasingly adept at the art of human husbandry since the genre 's inception in 1965 with The Dating Game . There 's little entertainment value in frictionless romance . Thanks to social @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of shame , producers can now efficiently cast contestants for maximum confrontation as well as compatibility . To heighten that emotional electricity , islanders share a bedroom and bathroom , spending the majority of their time in the golden prison of the villa where every movement is recorded . <p> No one questions the promulgation of certain Orwellian articles of faith . To find one 's true love , one must " stay open " to all other possible romantic encounters at all times . It 's virtuously " authentic " if such an encounter involves your smitten friend 's partner because " this is Love Island not Friendship Island " . But while contestants have left the outside world , they bring its values and stigmas . Caught between unrelenting pressure to form a monogamous bond and unrelenting pressure to seek the perfect upgrade , islanders find themselves in a combustible environment . <p> The average Love Island romance has the shelf life of spinach : " love " in the sense of fleeting magnetism between matching sets of bleached teeth . <p> Orwellian too are the glossy pretences @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all , and sex positivity in a toxically gendered milieu . Take the " body count " episode , where contestants disclose their prior sexual history . Or the " movie night " episode , where contestants are shown what was said and done behind their backs . In each , different consequences apply to the women -- viciously shamed by male contestants who accept those choices as normative for men . <p> This is called out as " ick " by the women , but it 's more than that . It speaks to dangerous imbalances in power and agency that are lethal in the real world and undermine the enabling egalitarian premise of the show . It raises questions of free consent around sexualised games and challenges -- the mixed make-out sessions , the private hideaway dates , the assumption that each woman is comfortable with being the passive pedestal for each man 's high-contact writhings during the " Hot Dawgs " male stripper challenge . But what if the conventions of the show do n't catalyse mutual attractions so much as apply social pressure to perform enthusiasm @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gets the respect of active consideration , we never see it . <p> The Orwellian mics and cameras have come a long way from the first seasons of Big Brother . They are embedded in make-up mirrors and trained on the shower and bodies in their beds , perpetually filming contestants doing everything from snacking to trimming their pubes . Yet despite the sheer volume of raw material , the luxuriant length of the show and many behind-the-scenes clips on social media , the picture of each islander that emerges in the edit is so thin it could float . As curated as the grid , viewers are served caricatured images that do n't get far past first impressions . <p> That 's to be expected from a show where contestants ' description of what they 're seeking in a partner begins and ends with muscle , bone and hair . The numbers indicate that superficiality is what this show 's audience wants . Love Island 's popularity means it would be a mistake not to take its lack of seriousness seriously . <p> While The Dating Game spawned celebrity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in 2005 , Britain 's Celebrity Love Island was axed for disappointing ratings . The second attempt , in 2015 , featured less recognisable faces and its popularity grew exponentially , spawning franchises from Finland to Argentina . But regardless of whether it 's filmed in Corfu or Cape Town , the villa remains the same : a place of pure possibility . <p> The average Love Island romance has the shelf life of spinach : " love " in the sense of fleeting magnetism between matching sets of bleached teeth . It 's perfect for ratings , TikTok and gaining a foothold for one 's personal branding endeavours . While season six might not deliver the expected love stories , it could deliver the greatest ones : genuine friendships . Taylor finds his " pookie bear " in " big little brother " Zane , with whom he looks forward to " creating content together , training together " . Mimi describes her bond with Sophie and Em as " the love of her life " . <p> In the end , however , the show 's most enduring @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Love IslandAustralia is apex trashy reality television : ethically dubious , well shot , propulsive and thriving . Its perpetual promise -- or pretence -- of love is the dramatic engine that powers the viewer to the end with such unrelenting momentum one barely notices that obscene amounts of time and attention have been spent on the long journey to nowhere . <p> While there 's sociological interest in its micro-world , group dynamics and the conditions under which the image-obsessed let their masks slip , high drama rather than complex veracity is the guiding value . Love Island 's high ratings offer no true insight into the perennial human curiosity about the lives of others -- the connective comforts of seeing our struggles in theirs . Instead , the fact that a global legion of viewers engages with this show suggests something far more unsettling . <p> Whether we love to hate it or hate to love it , the show 's hidden cameras reveal as much about us as they do the players ' flaws and insecurities , their palace intrigues , moments of loyalty , bullying and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's international uptake points to something primal . From our own incompatible drives for linking and ranking , to the power we invest in physical perfection , dream villas and fairytale endings , this is television that activates our deepest wish-fulfilment fantasies . Its transfixing popularity reminds us that we love to see people 's dreams come true almost as much as we love to see them shattered . <p> Love Island Australia is screening on 9NOW . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . Source : SBS News <p> Australia 's Pacific neighbour Nauru is selling passports to help cover the costs of moving thousands of residents from low-level homes threatened by climate change-induced floods and rising sea levels . <p> The passports will cost a minimum of US$130,000 ( $204,000 ) for a single applicant , US$137,500 ( $216,000 ) for a family of two to four , or US$145,000 ( $227,000 ) for a family of five or more . <p> The passport sales are part of the Nauru Economic and Climate Resilience Citizenship Program , which offers successful applicants a second citizenship and supports the island 's sustainable development . <h> Why is Nauru selling passports ? <p> The citizenship program aims to support global mobility , enabling passport holders @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ many people who buy Nauru passports may never visit the Pacific country , they will be able to travel to other destinations including Hong Kong , Ireland , Singapore , the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom . <h> READ MORE <p> Like other small islands in the South Pacific , Nauru is particularly vulnerable to the negative impacts of climate change . More than 80 per cent of Nauru 's land is considered uninhabitable , and it is facing more biodiversity loss and rising sea levels , which are threatening low-lying coastal areas . <p> To increase Nauru 's resilience , the government has established the Higher Ground Initiative ( HGI ) , which aims to migrate vulnerable homes and infrastructure to higher elevations . <p> It 's also working to expand local food production , restore degraded natural habitats and pioneer a new Pacific island urbanism . <p> According to Nauru 's Department of Climate Change and National Resilience , the HGI is a " generational undertaking " and " critical to long-term survival and viability of Nauru as a sovereign nation-state . " <p> It is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ action " . <h> What is Australia 's relationship with Nauru ? <p> As close neighbours , Australia and Nauru have an ongoing relationship , and Australia is Nauru 's largest economic , security and development partner . <p> In December 2024 , Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and President of Nauru David Waiau Ranibok Adeang signed the Nauru-Australia Treaty , which aims to help improve economic resilience and security . <p> Nauru is also home to an Australian offshore immigration detention facility , where asylum seekers who arrive by boat are sent . <h> READ MORE <p> In the 1960s , the Australian government proposed to relocate all Nauru residents to Curtis Island off the coast of Queensland . <p> This was due to the extensive damage done to Nauru through phosphate mining by Australian , New Zealand and British companies , which left much of the company devastated and led to scientists predicting it could become uninhabitable . <p> Australia would not release sovereignty over Curtis Island to Nauruans , but it would have allowed them to become Australian citizens . <p> Nauruans refused to go , and Nauru @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its own mines . <p> Nauru is selling passports as a fundraiser to help meet the costs of climate change . Source : AAP / Ben McKay <h> How is Australia supporting Pacific nations facing climate change ? <p> Nauru is one of several Pacific nations facing the devastating impacts of climate change , and Australia supports climate action in these areas through a series of initiatives and funding agreements . <p> These include the Climate and Oceans Support Program in the Pacific Phase 3 , the Australian Humanitarian Partnership Disaster READY Program , and the Pacific Resilience Facility . <p> In 2023 , Australia and Tuvalu also announced a bipartisan deal , under which Australia will take in 280 Tuvalu residents facing displacement from climate change each year . <p> Following the announcement , Foreign Minister Penny Wong said other nations in the region would be welcome to sign similar deals with Australia .

" <p> A third study published in the journal Environmental DNA sought to develop methods to track communities of fish in marine ecosystems including remote parts of the Great Australian Bight off the far west coast of South Australia @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ complementary in detecting different fish species . <p> One method used environmental DNA ( eDNA ) -- genetic material left behind by organisms as they swim through the water -- to estimate fish dispersal . @@121506646 <h> Light rail haters need to look at the bigger picture . This is making Canberra better <p> Australia has had an on-again , off-again relationship with light rail . <h> End of Summer Sale on now ! <p> or signup to continue reading <p> All articles from our website &amp; app <p> The digital version of Today 's Paper <p> Breaking news alerts direct to your inbox <p> Interactive Crosswords , Sudoku and Trivia <p> All articles from the other in your area <p> Once the backbone of transport in major cities during the 20th century , it was gradually sidelined by cars and buses and all but disappeared except for in Melbourne by the 1960s - at a time when our population was about 16 million less and we were not facing the impacts of climate change . <p> We now have unsustainable congestion and carbon emissions in our capital cities . <p> Thankfully , however , we are experiencing a light rail resurgence across the country , finally addressing this past error of judgment . <p> This revival reflects a global trend of rethinking urban transport - @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ - with a focus on sustainability , reducing congestion , and improving mobility . <p> The start of construction of the stage 2a extension of the Canberra light rail from Civic to Commonwealth Park , announced this week , marks an important step in Canberra 's journey towards the world-class transport that our capital city deserves and needs . <p> Just as Sir Walter Burley Griffin , the architect of Canberra , originally intended with a " tramway " system along Northbourne Avenue , connecting different areas of the city , as part of his city design nearly a century ago . <p> Despite the significant economic , environmental , and social benefits , there are still critics questioning the value of the light rail expansion in Canberra . <p> Yet , the evidence speaks for itself . <p> The Canberra light rail project will result in a major decrease in traffic in the long term . This is exactly the kind of transport investment Canberra needs to accommodate its growing population and encourage further urban renewal . <p> Stage 1 of the Canberra light rail has already revitalised Northbourne @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for urban development and attracting hundreds of millions of dollars in private investment . It has transformed the gateway into the capital , resulting in new housing projects , retail spaces , and community amenities . <p> This development promotes higher-density , sustainable living along transport corridors , making the surrounding neighbourhoods more vibrant and connected . <p> A 2020 government report on benefits arising from stage 1 of the Canberra Light Rail noted the replacement of 1288 aged public houses , providing tenants with newer , higher quality housing and that the " redevelopment of the corridor , particularly Northbourne Avenue is attracting new business and commercial operations , including the new ACT government office and mixed-use development at the Dickson interchange . " <p> Light rail 's special power is its ability to foster urban regeneration that delivers a multitude of positive social and environmental outcomes . <p> This is due to light rail 's ability to provide high frequency , turn-up-and-go connections between a range of mixed use , education , health , residential and special events precincts in a way that is quiet , safe and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ provide the certainty needed to support urban development and densification in a way that buses or trackless trams - whose routes can change at any time - can not . <p> It is also an easy , highly accessible mode that integrates seamlessly with cycling and walking paths for " last mile " travel , helping to ease traffic congestion . <p> According to ARA research , light rail can move between 4000 and 20,000 people per hour in space equivalent to one lane of road traffic . By comparison , the same lane can only move 800 cars ( or less than 1000 people ) per hour , and between 2000 and 8,000 people per hour on buses . <p> In other words , light rail moves significantly more people in the same space , making it a far more efficient mode of transport . <p> Sydney 's George Street has been transformed thanks to light rail . It was once congested with cars and is now a pedestrian-friendly hub filled with green spaces , public seating , and easy connections to other parts of the city like Circular @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rail is also compelling . Without intervention , the transport sector is set to become Australia 's largest source of emissions by 2030 . <p> Rail is a key player in our journey to net-zero emissions ( stage 1 of Canberra light rail achieved net zero ) . <p> While rail accounts for only 4 per cent of Australia 's transport emissions , road transport contributes 83 per cent and aviation 9 per cent . <p> By encouraging mode shift from cars to light rail , we can reduce emissions by about 30 per cent , making light rail an essential part of our environmental strategy . <p> A study released by the Canberra Urban Regional Futures established that the Canberra light rail would result in about 2,900 to 4,700 tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions per year being eliminated from the transport sector , translating to an 18 to 30 per cent emission reduction on the City to Gungahlin corridor in 2020 compared to business-as-usual . <p> It is clear that light rail plays a critical role in integrated transport networks , providing great placemaking potential and the ability to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> It is time the critics of the Canberra light rail consider the bigger picture and fully embrace its potential to shape a cleaner , more efficient , and more livable capital city . <p> Caroline Wilkie is the chief executive of the Australasian Railway Association .

@@121534361 <h> Leaning to the left <p> Young women are increasingly progressive . Young men -- particularly gen Z ( born after 1994 ) -- are leaning more conservative in many countries , including the United States , China , South Korea and Germany . <p> My analysis of the Australian data mirrors global trends , but with a twist . <p> Young Australian women are moving sharply to the left . But unlike in many other countries , young Australian men are also shifting left , just at a slower pace . <p> Australia 's leftward move across generations is reflected in both self-placement on a left-right ideological scale , and in the vote in federal elections . <p> In the 2022 Australian election , the Coalition received its lowest-ever share of the women 's vote at just 32% . Only 24.3% of millennials ( 21.9% of men and 25.7% of women ) voted for the Coalition in 2022 . <p> These are the lowest levels of support for either major party among younger people in the history of the survey . <p> Among gen Z , a slightly higher @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of men and 19.8% of women ) . <h> What 's driving this ? <p> In theory , women 's leftward shift is driven by several factors . These include higher education levels , greater participation in professional work , and exposure to feminist values . Despite Australia 's post-industrial , egalitarian image , persistent gendered inequalities and discrimination also play a role . <p> Meanwhile , young men 's move to the left can be attributed to progressive and egalitarian socialisation . Plus , unlike in other countries , Australia lacks Donald Trump-like figures who could mobilise anti-feminist or hardline conservative sentiments . This limits the expression of such views at an aggregate level . <p> This leftward shift is , in part , a generational effect -- or at least a reflection of the times . <p> The generational angle is crucial , as the 2025 federal election will be the first in which millennials and gen Z together will outnumber baby boomers as the dominant voting bloc in Australia . <p> This shift should shape how political parties campaign , who they target , and which issues @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ My analysis highlights another important angle . Over the study period , voting decisions have increasingly been driven by policy issues , with 48% of Australians citing them as the primary factor . This is followed by party affiliation ( 29% ) , party leaders ( 14% ) and local candidates ( 9% ) . <p> In 2022 , 54% of voters reported policy issues as the main factor influencing their choice . <p> Across election years , I identified the most prominent and recurrent election issues that voters identified as influential . I added these issues to my model to see how people who care about these issues lean ( left-right ) and whether men and women differ in their political leanings ( progressive-conservative ) . Highly educated , working-class , non-religious and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ too , do those raised in left-leaning households . <p> While the size of these effects varies slightly between men and women , the overall direction remains the same . <h> How might this play out in 2025 ? <p> The thing about election issues is that they are highly time-sensitive . Take the GST : it was one of the defining issues of the 1998 election , yet was largely irrelevant after 2004 . <p> In recent years , left-leaning issues -- the environment , health and Medicare -- were more likely to be front-of-mind when Australians all of ages headed to the polls . This gives Labor and the Greens an issue-owner advantage . <p> Cost of living ( spanning day-to-day expenses , interest rates and housing affordability ) has now become the defining issue of this election cycle . At first thought , among the two major parties , the Coalition is traditionally seen as a better economic manager . <p> However , my analysis of 2022 election data shows that , compared with the 2019 election , fewer people considered the Coalition the best manager of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ election issue . <p> Further , for the first time in the past five elections , a majority of the voters perceived Labor as more aligned with their own views on immigration , refugees and asylum seekers . These issues , historically seen as Coalition strongholds , are also likely to be key this time around . <p> For the Coalition , this is bad news . But for Labor , the challenge is twofold : retaining younger , progressive voters while addressing broader economic anxieties . <p> With growing voter volatility and a diminished sense of party loyalty , neither major party can rely on a stable base . <p> Australians are increasingly willing to shift allegiances , including to the increasing supply of independent alternatives . @@121545621 <h> Helen Haines How to regain public trust in the NACC <p> As we hurtle towards the next federal election , I often reflect on the months leading up to the last one . In those dying days of the Morrison government , the public and political push for a federal corruption watchdog was at its peak . <p> The lack of accountability for the devastating robodebt scandal and allegations of bullying and sexual assault at Parliament House left people angry and wanting to see justice done . As part of what was then a much smaller cross bench , I was fighting doggedly to push the government to establish a robust , independent federal integrity commission . <p> At every turn , it felt as if Scott Morrison sought to delay and distract to block our efforts . Without a doubt , his dismissal of the electorate 's desire for an anti-corruption commission with teeth cost him and his party at the polls . It was a critical issue in the historical success of independents at the last federal election . <p> A lot has changed in three years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Anti-Corruption Commission . <p> Well into the NACC 's second year of operation , following the release of its first annual report and first public hearing of the joint parliamentary oversight committee -- and with an election looming -- it 's time to reflect on how well the NACC is working . <p> Is it fulfilling its intention to expose corrupt conduct ? Is it living up to the public 's expectations to hold public officials accountable for misconduct ? Is it restoring public trust in government and politicians ? <p> These are thorny questions because the work of the NACC to date has been undertaken almost entirely behind closed doors . The decisions we do know about have left the commission open to criticism , including concerns about the lack of transparency and the restrictive " exceptional circumstances " test for public hearings . Australians are watching the NACC 's performance and expect it to deliver real accountability , not just symbolic reforms . <p> It is with this expectation in mind that we consider the NACC 's reversal , announced this week , of its initial decision not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by the Royal Commission into Robodebt . <p> That initial decision , from June last year , was an early misstep for the new commission . It drew more than 1000 complaints to the NACC inspector Gail Furness . Though the move by the independent reviewer , Geoffrey Nettle , KC , to relaunch investigations is welcome , we know little more at this stage about how or why this has come about . Now , as has been the case throughout its short life , the NACC 's workings are largely invisible to a concerned public . <p> Robodebt , and the investigation into the government contractor Paladin , were the NACC 's highest-profile cases , but certainly not the only ones the NACC has handled in its first 18 months or so of operation . @@121545636 <h> David Ritter WA must not dictate nature policy <p> I 've never heard an Australian politician admit to being in favour of extinction . This visual stillness is an interrogation of silence , an examination of what is being left unsaid both by Julie and the adults around her . Through careful watching and the distinct rhythm of its compositions , Julie Keeps Quiet captures a culture of complicity , the weight of a difficult situation and a slow shift in its protagonist . <p> This unwavering , formal approach puts Julie Keeps Quiet in stark comparison with the most high-profile film about tennis from the past year , Luca Guadagnino 's Challengers . That film 's playful , hyper-stylised filmmaking was filled with flamboyant movement , including memorably occupying the point-of-view of a tennis ball . Sex and tennis were conflated , made indivisible , its comic depiction of competitiveness becoming a study of shifting power in personal and romantic relationships . The collisions of sex , tennis and power are present in Julie Keeps Quiet but explored on an institutional level and played -- and underplayed -- for drama rather than comedy . <p> This @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its attendant power imbalance -- between a domineering coach and an obsessive pupil , something powerfully chronicled in another Belgian work , Charl ? ne Favier 's 2020 film Slalom ( which stars J ? r ? mie Renier , an actor forever associated with the Dardennes ) . Source : Queensland Government <h> Why are mangroves so important in places like Brisbane ? <p> Mangroves are critical to coastal ecosystems , especially in areas like Brisbane and the broader Moreton Bay region , where they play a key role in environmental stability , biodiversity , and climate resilience . Destroying them @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as natural buffers against coastal erosion , storm surges , and rising sea levels . Their dense root systems stabilise shorelines , preventing land loss during extreme weather events like cyclones and king tides , which are common in southeast Queensland . When mangroves are destroyed , coastal areas become more vulnerable to flooding and erosion . <p> Mangroves are carbon sinks , absorbing and storing large amounts of carbon dioxide . They sequester up to four times more carbon than tropical rainforests per hectare , helping to reduce greenhouse gas levels . When they are removed , the stored carbon is released back into the atmosphere . <p> They also act as natural filters , trapping sediments , heavy metals , and pollutants before they reach open water . This helps maintain the water quality of rivers , estuaries , and Moreton Bay , benefiting both marine life and humans . @@121612078 <h> I looked at 35 years of data to see how Australians vote <p> In the 2022 federal election , two demographics were key to the final outcome : women and young people . <h> End of Summer Sale on now ! <p> or signup to continue reading <p> All articles from our website &amp; app <p> The digital version of Today 's Paper <p> Breaking news alerts direct to your inbox <p> Interactive Crosswords , Sudoku and Trivia <p> All articles from the other in your area <p> With another election fast approaching , will they swing the result again ? <p> To answer this question , I turned to the Australian Election Study ( AES ) data spanning the period from 1987 to 2022 , to investigate how different demographics have voted over time . <p> I found that , generally , Australian women and young people tend to favour left-of-centre parties . <p> However , specific election issues can have a substantial impact , making the political context of each election crucial . So what can we expect this time around ? <h> Leaning to the left @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ between the sexes worldwide . <p> Young women are increasingly progressive . Young men - particularly Gen Z ( born after 1994 ) - are leaning more conservative in many countries , including the United States , China , South Korea and Germany . <p> My analysis of the Australian data mirrors global trends , but with a twist . <p> Young Australian women are moving sharply to the left . But unlike in many other countries , young Australian men are also shifting left , just at a slower pace . <p> Australia 's leftward move across generations is reflected in both self-placement on a left-right ideological scale , and in the vote in federal elections . <p> In the 2022 Australian election , the Coalition received its lowest-ever share of the women 's vote at just 32 per cent . <p> History can tell us how different generations tend to vote . Pictures The Canberra Times , Shutterstock <p> Only 24.3 per cent of Millennials ( 21.9 per cent of men and 25.7 per cent of women ) voted for the Coalition in 2022 . <p> These are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ younger people in the history of the survey . <p> Among Gen Z , a slightly higher proportion of 24.6 per cent voted for the Coalition ( 34.0 per cent of men and 19.8 per cent of women ) . <h> What 's driving this ? <p> In theory , women 's leftward shift is driven by several factors . These include higher education levels , greater participation in professional work , and exposure to feminist values . Despite Australia 's post-industrial , egalitarian image , persistent gendered inequalities and discrimination also play a role . <p> Meanwhile , young men 's move to the left can be attributed to progressive and egalitarian socialisation . Plus , unlike in other countries , Australia lacks Donald Trump-like figures who could mobilise anti-feminist or hardline conservative sentiments . This limits the expression of such views at an aggregate level . <p> This leftward shift is , in part , a generational effect - or at least a reflection of the times . <p> The generational angle is crucial , as the 2025 federal election will be the first in which Millennials and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ voting bloc in Australia . <p> This shift should shape how political parties campaign , whom they target , and which issues take centre stage . <h> Policies are voter priorities <p> My analysis highlights another important angle . Over the study period , voting decisions have increasingly been driven by policy issues , with 48 per cent of Australians citing them as the primary factor . This is followed by party affiliation ( 29 per cent ) , party leaders ( 14 per cent ) and local candidates ( 9 per cent ) . <p> In 2022 , 54 per cent of voters reported policy issues as the main factor influencing their choice . <p> Across election years , I identified the most prominent and recurrent election issues that voters identified as influential . I added these issues to my model to see how people who care about these issues lean ( left-right ) and whether men and women differ in their political leanings ( progressive-conservative ) . I also considered other factors known to impact voting , including : <p> social network factors ( whether they 're religious @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( what each respondent said were the most important voting issues ) <p> Overall , women tend to be slightly more left-leaning on policy issues than men , and while this difference is statistically significant , it is small and the general trend holds across both sexes . <p> Compared with Boomers , each successive generation is more likely to vote for a left party . Gen Z is the most left-leaning ( though their smaller sample size warrants some caution in interpretation ) . <h> So who votes for whom ? <p> Unsurprisingly , people vote according to who they think will best address the policy areas they care about most . <p> Those prioritising interest rates , taxation or economic management favour right-wing parties . Voters most concerned with health , Medicare and climate change are more likely to vote for the left . <p> Education , class and social networks matter , too . Highly educated , working-class , non-religious and union-affiliated voters tend to support left parties . So , too , do those raised in left-leaning households . <p> While the size of these effects @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ remains the same . <h> How might this play out in 2025 ? <p> The thing about election issues is that they are highly time-sensitive . Take the GST : it was one of the defining issues of the 1998 election , yet was largely irrelevant after 2004 . <p> In recent years , left-leaning issues - the environment , health and Medicare - were more likely to be front-of-mind when Australians all of ages headed to the polls . This gives Labor and the Greens an issue-owner advantage . <p> Cost of living ( spanning day-to-day expenses , interest rates and housing affordability ) has now become the defining issue of this election cycle . At first thought , among the two major parties , the Coalition is traditionally seen as a better economic manager . <p> However , my analysis from 2022 election data shows that , compared with the 2019 election , fewer people considered the Coalition the best manager of the economy among those who considered it the most important election issue . <p> Further , for the first time in the past five elections , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with their own views on immigration , refugees and asylum seekers . These issues , historically seen as Coalition strongholds , are also likely to be key this time around . <p> For the Coalition , this is bad news . But for Labor , the challenge is twofold : retaining younger , progressive voters while addressing broader economic anxieties . <p> With growing voter volatility and a diminished sense of party loyalty , neither major party can rely on a stable base . <p> Australians are increasingly willing to shift allegiances , including to the increasing supply of independent alternatives . Both Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Peter Dutton will have to convince voters they have the best solutions for the key issues . <p> Intifar Chowdhury is lecturer in government , Flinders University . This article first appeared in The Conversation .

@@121613265 <h> Manipulated media : The weapon of the Right <p> The re-election of Donald Trump is proof that the Right 's most powerful weapon is media manipulation , ensuring the public sphere is not engaged in rational debate , writes Dr Victoria Fielding . <p> I ONCE HEARD someone say that when the Left and the Right became polarised -- when they divorced from each other -- the Left got all the institutions of truth including science , education , justice and democratic government . The Right got the institution of manipulation : the media . This statement hit me for six at the time because it seemed so clearly true . <p> What was also immediately clear is that there was an obvious reason why the Left sided with the institutions of truth and the Right resorted to manipulation . It is because truth does not suit right-wing arguments . <p> The existence of climate change does not suit fossil fuel billionaires . Evidence that wealth does not trickle down does not suit the capitalist class . The idea that diversity , equity and inclusion ( yes , I @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ better for everyone , rather than a discriminatory , hateful , destructive , divided unequal world is dangerous for the Right to admit . <p> The Right 's embrace of the media institution also makes sense when you consider that the institutions of truth are difficult to buy , whereas billionaires can easily own manipulative media . Just ask Elon Musk , who bought Twitter and turned it into a political manipulation machine . Just ask Rupert Murdoch , who is currently engaged in a bitter family war to stop three of his children opposing him and his son Lachlan from using their " news " organisations as a form of political manipulation for right-wing interests . <p> Right-wingers also know that truthful institutions only have one way of communicating their truths to the public : via the media . Once the media environment is manipulated , we enter a post-truth world . <p> This is the world where billionaire fossil fuel interests undermine climate action . It is where scientists create vaccines to save lives but the manipulated public refuses to take them . Where experts are derided as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ whole idea of democratic government in the U.S. has been overthrown to install an autocratic billionaire-enriching oligarchy led by an incompetent fool who calls himself the King . <p> Once you recognise this manipulated media environment , you also understand that there is not -- and never has been -- such as thing as a rational public debate . Those engaged in the institutions of the Left -- in science , education , justice and democratic government -- seem mostly unwilling to accept this fact . Instead , they continue to believe if they just keep telling people the truth and communicating what they see as entirely rational arguments , the public will accept what they have to say . <p> I think part of the reason that the Left refuses to accept that public debate is not rational and rather , is a manipulated bin fire of misleading information , including mis/disinformation and propaganda , is because they are not equipped to compete in this reality . What do those on the Left do with " post-truth " ? They seem to just want to ignore it and hope @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ misunderstanding of the post-truth world and the manipulated media environment 's impact on the public is this paper , by political science professors at the Australian National University Ian McAllister and Nicholas Biddle . <p> Their research sought to understand why polling at the start of the 2023 Indigenous Voice to Parliament Referendumshowed widespread public support for the Voice but over the course of the campaign , this support dropped to the point where the Voice was defeated with 60 per cent voting " No " and 40 per cent , " Yes " . <p> In presenting their study 's findings , the authors make the stunningly absolutist claim that : <p> ' ... the public 's exposure to all forms of mass media -- as we have measured it here -- had no impact on the result ' . <p> A note is then attached to this finding with the caveat : <p> ' As noted earlier , given the data at hand we are unable to test the possibility that the content of the media being consumed resulted in a reinforcement of existing beliefs and partisanship rather @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gaping hole in the finding by failing to account for how media reinforcing existing beliefs is an important media effect -- as argued by Neil Gavin here . Since it was not measured , how can they possibly say there was no effect ? <p> Furthermore , the very premise of the author 's sweeping statement that media exposure had no impact on the result of the Referendum is based on two naive assumptions : <p> that voters were rational in their deliberations over the Referendum question ; and <p> that the information environment voters were presented with was rational . <p> This dual assumption of rationality -- one that the authors interestingly admit is an assumption -- is evidenced in their hypothesis which states : <p> ' Voters who did not follow the campaign in the mass media were more likely to move from a yes to a no vote compared to voters who did follow the campaign in the mass media . ' <p> This hypothesis , the authors explain , is premised on the assumption ' that those with less information are more likely to opt for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and therefore that less exposure to media would change a vote from " Yes " to " No " . <p> What this hypothesis assumes is that if a voter received more rational information in the media about the Referendum , that information would rationally drive their vote in the " Yes " direction . When their data disproved this hypothesis , the authors used this finding to claim that the media had no effect . <p> To understand the reality of what happened in the Referendum debate , the word " rational " needs to be taken out of the equation and the word " manipulated " put in . <p> We know , of course , that the Referendum was awash with manipulative information , which all supported the " No " campaign . For example , my study of News Corp 's Voice coverage -- Australia 's largest and most influential news organisation -- found that News Corp actively campaigned for the " No " proposition in concert with the " No " campaign , presenting content more like a political campaign than traditional journalism and commentary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Tim Graham analysed how the Voice Referendum was discussed on social media platform , X. Far from a rational debate , Graham identified that the " No " campaign and its supporters engaged in a participatory disinformation propaganda campaign , which became a " truth market " about the Voice . This " truth market " was described as drawing " Yes " campaigners into a debate about the truth of the Voice , sidetracking them from promoting their own cause . <p> What such studies showed was that , far from McAllister and Biddle 's assumed rational information environment , the Voice Referendum public debate was awash with manipulation , propaganda , disinformation and fear-mongering . The " No " campaign that delivered this manipulation perfectly demonstrates how the Right uses media to undermine institutions of truth , to undermine facts and to undermine the rationality of democratic debates . <p> The completely unfounded assumption that the more information a voter received about the Voice , the more likely they would vote " Yes " , reveals a misunderstanding of the reality of a manipulated public debate environment present @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ social media . <p> It also wrongly treats voters like rational deliberative computers by assuming that the more information that goes in , the more they accept that information . This is far from the reality of how mediated communication affects the public . <p> The reason the influence of media on individuals and collectives is , in reality , so difficult to measure and should never be bluntly described as having total effect or no effect , is that people are not rational when they consume media , and every individual processes information in their own unique and unconscious ways . One person can watch a manipulated piece of communication and accept it wholeheartedly , others can accept part of it and others reject it outright . <p> No one piece of information determines how people vote and not every piece of information people consume does either . That 's the point of a manipulated media environment . People who are being manipulated do not know they are being manipulated . <p> Importantly , when you ask individuals how their media consumption impacted them , they of course do @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ information they have ephemerally consumed -- whether from the media , conversations , or a wide range of other information sources , are incredibly complex and irrational . <p> Surely the re-election of Donald Trump for a second time , despite all the rational arguments against him , is proof that the manipulated media environment is an incredibly powerful weapon -- a weapon the Right , globally , is clearly proficient at wielding . It is time those on the Left caught up and at least understood the reality they are working in.

On Queensland 's Heron Island , when nest temperature rises above 29.1oC Green Sea Turtle hatchlings are all female . <p> Western Australian loggerhead turtles ' pivotal temperature ( PT ) is 28.7oC -- the PT is the nest temperature at which you 'll get equal numbers of males and females -- higher temperatures mean more females . <p> " In far North Queensland we have seen the world 's largest green turtle rookery producing a 99 per cent female population due to a warming climate , it also @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ University Senior Research Fellow , Dr Rachel Groom . <p> Mollie Rickwood <p> Turtles also return to nest at the same beaches from which they hatched , which makes populations vulnerable to global heating . <p> University of Exeter researchers were able to explore questions of temperature 's effect on nesting responses of Green Sea Turtles through analysis of their 31-year data set focussed on a turtle population which nests every year on a North Cyprus beach in the Mediterranean . <p> The dataset contained information on more than 600 individual turtles , collected during nesting seasons from mid-May to mid-August from 1992 to 2023 . @@121654759 <h> What 's next for BHP ? The moment is ripe for copper 's biggest deal <h> By David Fickling <h> Save articles for later <p> In times of plenty , you can afford to be picky . When scarcity stalks the land , you may have to lower your standards . <p> That 's a lesson for BHP as it scours the globe looking for ways to fill a looming deficit of copper , with the energy transition stoking demand for the conductive metal . <p> BHP is pivoting to copper as iron ore demand has peaked.Credit : BHP <p> The world 's biggest mining company is in the process of turning itself into a copper miner from an iron ore one . Five years ago , iron ore accounted for as much as 85 per cent of earnings and 39 per cent of capital spending . In the years ahead , that will flip . It plans to dedicate roughly half of its capex to copper , pushing iron ore below a quarter of the total . <p> The problem is the dearth of good deposits to spend @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ them are locked up in unattractive jurisdictions . That 's particularly difficult for BHP . Despite having arguably the biggest war chest , it has a reputation for being the least buccaneering of the large miners . <p> Glencore has major units in exotic locations such as Kazakhstan and the Democratic Republic of Congo , and Rio Tinto is developing copper projects in Mongolia and iron ore in Guinea . BHP sticks to a more staid and stable set of jurisdictions : Australia , Brazil , Canada , Chile , Peru and the US . When it made a $US49 billion ( $79 billion ) failed bid for Anglo American last year , it was carefully structured to excise any units from the target 's historic home market , South Africa . <p> BHP can afford to think bigger . Right now , major mining M&amp;A is in the air . <p> There are advantages to that . Dicey politics can be both an operational and reputational risk . Rio Tinto 's 28-year quest to develop its Guinean iron ore mine has cost it the careers of several top executives @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ billion in 2022 to settle bribery and market-manipulation charges , while Switzerland last month jailed the former chief operating officer of commodity trader Trafigura Beheer in a bribery case . <p> The downside is that the world 's best mineral resources did n't conveniently place themselves in the most congenial addresses . That consideration will encourage any miner to look well beyond its backyard . <p> Even BHP has been venturing outside of its comfort zone of late . In Argentina -- a country long considered off-limits to major miners due to its unattractive political and legal backdrop -- it last month completed a $US2 billion deal to buy its way into half of the Filo del Sol copper project alongside Lundin Mining . That 's been helped by a more favourable set of mining laws under libertarian President Javier Milei , but still represents a significant long-term wager on a jurisdiction synonymous with ever-changing policy and economic conditions . <p> Advertisement <p> Loading <p> BHP can afford to think bigger , though . Right now , major mining M&amp;A is in the air . Glencore and Rio Tinto have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ largest in industry history . That suggests the moment is ripe for a combination BHP has long contemplated , but always shied away from : A bid for Freeport-McMoRan , the biggest copper miner of all . <p> Such a tie-up would double BHP 's production of the red metal overnight and give it four of the five biggest copper mines , but still leave it with less than 20 per cent of global mined supply , well below levels that should trigger competition concerns . <p> The downside of any such deal has always been the whiff of sketchy governance that hangs around Grasberg , Freeport 's biggest mine . Located high in the remote mountains of Indonesia 's half of New Guinea , it 's situated in a region that has long been synonymous with clashes between separatist groups and Jakarta 's security forces , many of the latter funded by Grasberg 's owners as site protection . <p> On top of that , mining waste is dumped into rivers flowing down toward the sea -- not a good look for BHP , which has been plagued over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Tedi copper-gold mine over the border in Papua New Guinea , and the Samarco iron ore project in Brazil . <p> BHP chief executive Mike Henry would do well to strike while the copper is hot . <p> Those issues are enough to give a cautious miner pause . But the political risks around Grasberg have diminished of late . Years of tense negotiations between Freeport and Jakarta concluded in 2018 , giving a state-owned company a majority stake and reducing the risk of expropriation . It 's been nearly five years since separatist violence claimed a life within Grasberg 's immense operational area , a region roughly the size of Rhode Island . <p> Loading <p> Freeport has also worked to turn around its poor reputation . These days , it scores highly ( better than BHP , in fact ) in a ranking of resource companies ' human rights performance by the World Benchmarking Alliance , a corporate responsibility non-profit . In 2023 , Freeport and Grasberg were awarded the Copper Mark , an industry label intended to promote responsibly sourced metal that gave the tick of approval @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ greatest mineral deposits can be exploited for decades or even centuries , but the opportunity to buy them only comes up once in a generation . <p> For BHP , that moment may finally have arrived . Henry would do well to strike while the copper is hot . <p> David Fickling is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering climate change and energy . Previously , he worked for Bloomberg News , the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times .

The warning came with a recommendation to either radically reduce the number of farmed salmon in the harbour or environmental remediation strategies to increase the amount of oxygen in the water . <p> If the skate becomes extinct , it would be the highest profile extinction for Tasmania since the Thylacine or Tasmanian tiger in the 1930s . Here , in alphabetical order only , is the 2025 CMO Power List . <h> Amanda McVay <h> Coles <p> Amanda McVay , chief customer officer ( CCO ) at Coles , brings a wealth of retail experience and a customer-first philosophy to one of Australia 's leading supermarket chains . <p> With a career spanning more than two decades in merchandising , commercial , and supply chain roles in the US , McVay has transformed her deep analytical expertise into a data-driven and empathetic approach to marketing and customer engagement . <p> Joining Coles 18 months ago , McVay 's path to her current role was anything but conventional . " Most of my career was spent on the commercial and financial side of retail , " she explained . <p> " I transitioned to marketing only in the last few years , driven by a fascination with consumer behaviour and why choices were made , and all the different influencers and indicators to try to help best predict how customers may make their next choice . " <p> Central to McVay 's strategy is a focus on customer needs , particularly during challenging economic times . <p> " The cost-of-living crisis is a significant concern for Australians right now , and we 're deeply aware of our role in helping families stretch their budgets , " she said . <p> " We 're here to solve problems for our customers and make their lives a little easier , " she added . <p> " We really feel that it 's our responsibility to serve customers in this time . " <p> McVay also sees segmentation as a cornerstone of retail marketing . <p> " What sets retailers apart is the ability to segment customers based on purchasing behaviour rather than demographics , " she explained . <p> " It 's not just about who they are but what they buy and how they shop . That allows us to personalise experiences and make shopping more relevant . " <p> Digital marketing and social media are key tools in her strategy . McVay is particularly interested in how these platforms inspire and influence customer behaviour . <p> " Social media is where consumers discover new ideas and products , " she said . <p> " We 're learning how to show up authentically in that space , using user-generated content and influencers to build trust and engagement . " <p> Beyond marketing , McVay has helped deepen Coles ' community connections , especially through sports sponsorships . Recent initiatives including partnerships with Football Australia and Little Athletics have reinforced the company 's commitment to local communities . <p> " It 's about more than sponsorship -- it 's about enabling families to connect through sport , even during tough times , " she said . <p> While sustainability is n't yet a focal point in Coles ' external campaigns , McVay noted that the company is working hard behind the scenes . <p> " Customers want proof points when it comes to sustainability -- we want to make sure we can demonstrate that with those specific products as much as possible , more so than general statements . " <p> Leadership is another area where McVay shines . Described as a collaborative and empowering leader , she spends significant time working closely with her team . <p> " I believe in aligning on priorities and giving my team the freedom to execute , " she explained . <p> " I 'm also a big proponent of cross-functional collaboration because success in retail requires everyone to work together . " <p> Despite the challenges of leading marketing for a major supermarket in turbulent times , McVay remains focused on Coles ' mission to support Australian families . <p> " It is a tough time for consumers in Australia , cost of living is a real issue and we play a very critical role in that " . <p> " We really feel that it 's our responsibility to serve customers in this time " . <p> With a blend of analytical rigour , creative vision and a deep commitment to customers , McVay is helping Coles navigate today 's challenges while building a stronger , more connected future . <h> Anneliese Douglass <h> Nestl ? <p> Anneliese Douglass has served as Nestl ? ' s director of marketing and communications for a shade over three years . Her role is vast , covering brands from Nescaf ? and Nespresso to Maggi , MILO and Smarties . <p> But it also covers a huge swathe of the southern hemisphere . Douglass is responsible for Australia , New Zealand and thousands of islands across the Pacific . To give you a sense of the role it 's more than 7,700km from her Sydney office to the Pitcairn Islands -- or Sydney to Perth and back with some change . <p> Managing that would be enough to make anyone 's head spin . But for Douglass , everything comes down to perspective , planning and leadership . <p> " We have an extraordinary team ... but because we 're so busy , we have a list of priority big bets that we have coming for the year . The business knows that 's where we 're putting our resources , our energy and our focus , " Douglass said . <p> " Then I 'll focus on some key areas -- for me what 's really important is driving a culture of creativity and creativity of work . But digital transformation is super important to me , it gives our marketers the fuel and the time they need to think strategically and creatively . " <p> Setting a business of Nestl ? ' s size and complexity on a digital transformation is no easy task . It might be as simple as making Microsoft Excel forms interactive but it could also be as complex as harnessing the latest AI advancement to deepen its consumer insights . And remember , that 's happening across multiple brands , in multiple verticals in multiple countries at the same time . <p> " Anything that is about change , sticking your head above the parapet can sometimes cause a headache . But that 's what true leadership is . " <p> However , given the scale of the task that Douglass has on her hands , her role is as much about gathering , organising and empowering diverse teams to deliver dispersed outcomes as it is getting into the weeds . <p> " I 'm a very big believer in having specialist functions within marketing . You need specialist expertise . I ca n't always go deep in digital . I know the vision and what I want but I need the specialist expertise to get me there . It 's not left brain-right brain , I need to have different people in my team to help me deliver it , " she said . <p> Douglass ' humility in her leadership is noticeable , particularly when she is proving an exemplar to the rest of the industry on social matters . For instance , Nestl ? ' s KitKat brand partnered with the 36 Months campaign and Nestle was a founding member of Ad Net Zero . <p> " For us , we 've done so much work on sustainability with our supply chain partners , recycled materials and more . It made perfect sense for us to focus more on marketing ... I had felt a bit alone in the discussions on advertising and marketing because we did n't have anything like Ad Net Zero , when I would have discussions with suppliers , agencies and so on , you 're kind of working it out for yourself . Now , we can all learn from each other and collaborate , " said Douglass . <p> " Anything that is about change , sticking your head above the parapet can sometimes cause a headache . But that 's what true leadership is , saying ' This is right for us and our organisation ' . <p> " From my point of view , you do n't have to do this in marketing and advertising -- but it 's the right thing to do , " Douglass added . <p> We could all learn more than a thing or two from Douglass ' leadership in the space . Our planet depends on it , after all . <h> Brent Smart <h> Telstra <p> Brent Smart has been among Australia 's leading marketers for a while , having served as the CMO of IAG before joining Telstra in 2022 . Before that , he spent three years as CEO of Saatchi &amp; Saatchi New York with stops at BBDO San Francisco , Colenso BBDO and M&amp;C Saatchi . It 's some CV , to say the least . <p> He has overseen a complete reimagining of the Telstra brand and perhaps a vertical . What if your telco could be cool -- like genuinely cool ? <p> " It 's a bit of a soundbite of mine but if you want to change how people feel about a brand , change how the brand feels . And we 've massively changed how the brand feels , " Smart told B&amp;T . <p> " The group that are noticing the new Telstra is the group that is hardest to move : non-customers . We had a big gap between our customers and non-customers . Our customers think we 're doing a pretty good job and it 's this entrenched brand perception amongst non-customers that 's really hard to move and we 're noticing that starting to move . Its largest rival , Optus has still not fully recovered from its 2022 data breach brand disaster . Its 2023 outage , which ultimately led to CEO Kelly Bayer Rosmarin resigning , did n't help either . But it is this context that allows Telstra to have such potent marketing . Its network did n't go down . Its customer 's data was n't hacked . <p> " Our network gets massive global acclaim . We 're one of the best networks in the world . We 've had something like 60 world firsts on the Telstra network . The Telstra app , he explained , gets " fantastic " customer ratings , for instance . <p> " On many rational aspects , we perform really well . I 'm trying to inject some emotion into the brand and ultimately into the experience . I want Telstra staff to be proud to work for Telstra . I want our customers to feel proud -- it 's a big word , man , to be proud of your telco . <p> " Ultimately , you 've got to get beyond the rational . Think about human behaviour and how people make purchase decisions , it is n't rational -- parts of it are rational , most of it 's emotional . You 've got to find a way to communicate emotionally and it 's even more importantly if you 're in a boring category . You 'd better find a way to be entertaining because no one is coming to your category with a level of interest . The idea of bringing entertainment is really important . <h> Chris Brown <h> McDonald 's Australia <p> When McDonald 's marketing boss Chris Brown first thought about the highlights 2024 would deliver , bringing a large purple monster and a lion to Aussie shores might not have been top of mind , but that 's exactly what has happened . <p> The Golden Arches delivered two of Australia 's most memorable and award winning marketing moments by rebooting the nostalgic Big Mac Chant for a new generation of Macca 's fans and also rekindling Grimace . <p> Brown , who took the helm of McDonald 's Australia 's marketing in 2020 before being elevated to chief customer officer in 2022 , is in a purple patch , if you 'll pardon the Grimace-shaped pun . <p> " Australians are doing it really , really tough and it 's something we are acutely aware of because McDonald 's is famous for value , " he said . <p> " Things like Grimace allows customers to escape some of the tough things that they 're dealing with by coming to McDonald 's and having a fun experience that delivers on value and is good for business . " <p> The campaign picked up the B&amp;T awards for Best Use of Tech &amp; AI and Best Radio/Audio campaign . " <h> Dean Norbiato <h> KIA <p> KIA 's Dean Norbiato hails from Griffith in the north-western Riverina region of New South Wales . " <p> That Aussie flavour sure did the trick when it came to lifting consideration , intent , brand love and loyalty . <p> " That campaign delivered the biggest single rise in brand metrics across all of our markers , of any period of time , that we 've ever had as a brand , " said Norbiato . <p> The KIA Tasman officially launches in Australia this year and KIA is eyeing a 10 per cent share of the uber-competitive ute market . " <h> Jenni Dill <h> Arnotts <p> When it comes to modernising an iconic Australian brand , the task requires both reverence for tradition and bold innovation . @@121698498 <p> The term ' public goods ' is well understood in the language of economics . Loosely , public goods are goods and services that can not be provided efficiently by private markets . <p> Textbooks define the term more precisely . They are goods and services that are ' non-rivalrous ' in consumption ( the supply is not depleted by consumption ) and ' non-excludable ' ( all people can take advantage of ) . Examples are national defence and street lighting . Public goods include not only tangible things like public roads but also services like town planning that reserves space for future roads and institutions such as the police , who enforce compliance in the name of road safety for all . <p> A wide range of the services and institutional arrangements essential for well-being are public goods , as we shall discuss in the next article . Here , I shall endeavour to pin down the essential nature of the concept . <p> Like many other concepts in policy discourse sufficiently understood to be useful , such as the ' rational self-interested individual ' , ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Right ' description of political affiliation , upon close examination the concept of public goods dissolves into fog . Here are six intricacies that cloud the textbook concept . <p> First , services can become congested so one or both of the ' non-rivalrous ' or ' non-excludable ' conditions can not be satisfied . In fact , it is difficult to identify many ' pure ' public goods . Parks can become packed with visitors , fresh air exhausted by automobiles and sunlight blocked by high-rise towers . Centrelink payments are non-rivalrous because the government will appropriate whatever money is needed to pay the legislatively specified entitlement . They are partially non-excludable because anyone who meets a certain threshold can take advantage . But long queues at Centrelink offices and onerous ' mutual obligation ' conditions prevent people from taking advantage , which means that the benefits are no longer an unambiguous public good . Robodebt drove a stake through the heart of the ' public goodness ' of welfare payments . <p> Second , an understanding of the concept can become bogged down in differentiating abstract from concrete @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ benefits from education as knowledge cascades through society and multiplies achievement . A government school can be called a public good because anyone can attend . But facilities can become overloaded by numbers and teachers overloaded by misbehaving students . These shortcomings are n't overcome by shifting the scale of the public good to the abstract ' education ' , because education can be privatised and private schools erect barriers to entry . <p> Third , extensive outsourcing during the past 40 years to the private sector of the provision of public goods on behalf of governments has muddied the definition . For example , Medicare is a public good that was established to enable every citizen to access free health care . At inception , every citizen was allowed free admission to a public hospital and consultation with a medical practitioner . Demand soon exceeded supply from government hospitals and public clinics , so successive governments fostered private health insurance which allowed citizens to access treatment in private hospitals with co-payments above basic Medicare payments . Similarly for consultations with specialist and general medical practitioners . Personal health services @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ occurring in public hospitals and clinics , thereby providing improvements in the health of the community albeit providing earlier access to citizens able to co-pay for non-emergency care . This combination of government and private health services effectively delivers a public good to the whole community . <p> Delivery by either governments or markets does not map neatly onto the definitions of public versus private good . Public goods are supplied not only by governments but also by individuals , not-for-profit organisations and commercial firms . Markets undersupply public goods because non-payers can not be excluded from enjoying the benefits ( called the ' free-rider ' problem ) . Private markets rely upon a direct connection between what people pay and the goods and services they receive . However , firms can produce public goods by philanthropy , through pre-payment by advertisers , as a by-product of their commercial operations , or under contract or instruction from governments . A firm that cleans up pollution or places useful information in the Internet 's public domain is generating a public good . <p> Fourth , many services that satisfy the textbook @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to all and are rarely crowded out can only hesitatingly be described as a public good . Delivered by corporations funded by advertising , they reflect the values and motives of the advertisers , not necessarily the public well-being . The consequences for public well-being of advertising by companies selling junk food , alcohol and gambling are sufficiently pernicious that they warrant stronger regulation in the public interest . <p> Fifth , the free gifts of nature are sometimes referred to as public goods . This may have been valid when human populations were smaller and natural resources appeared to be inexhaustible . Ocean fisheries for example that used to be available for all can nowadays be both depleted and rendered exclusive through licensing ( privatisation ) . Sunlight is a public good until somebody erects a high-rise tower block next to your boundary . Then there is climate change ! <p> Sixth , individuals can be excluded from many goods from which they should not be excluded . Scientific knowledge and the Internet are examples . In principle , they should be freely available for the benefit of world @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . In practice , e it is possible to partly commodify or privatise them by making them accessible only to those prepared to pay , such as through licence fees or sponsorship or by purchasing journals or equipment . Large publishing houses have commodified many journals and charge substantial fees for content that is provided to them free of charge by researchers ( or nowadays even at the cost of the researchers -- through author charges ) . The subscriptions that university libraries are required to pay to access journals online are now commonly restricted to students and academics of that university , denied to independent scholars who used to be able to browse the shelves of print journals free of charge , a lost public good . <h> A short political history <p> In the Western democracies after the early 1970s , neoliberal economics became the dominant economic ideology . Its simple coherence and appeal to the politically powerful led to the widespread downsizing of government agencies , intensifying the undersupply of public goods . This particularly disadvantages the poor , who lack enough purchasing power to obtain substitutes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ upon public goods : as the definition makes clear , all citizens benefit . Anyway , private markets can not function effectively unless certain public goods such as prudential regulation , contract law , criminal justice and physical infrastructure are adequately supplied . <h> Implications for policy <p> How is this discussion relevant to public health ? It is pivotal , because collective funding , not commercial funding , lies at the heart of the provision of public goods . Collective funding is derived from public budgets fed by taxation , from community effort , from philanthropy or in some cases from advertising . If collective funding falters , the availability of the public goods falters . <p> Governments may , with care and skill , outsource the provision of many public goods . But governments can not outsource their responsibility to ensure that public goods are actually provided . <p> The tendency of low-taxing , small-government societies to produce conditions of " private affluence and public squalor " , that is , an undersupply of public goods , was publicised by Canadian economist J.K. Galbraith in The Affluent Society @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> That crisply describes Australia 's contemporary condition : private affluence enjoyed by half the population , impoverishment seeping through the other half and chronic insufficiency of funding for departments delivering public goods . Education , leisure , parks , environmental protection , corporate regulation and a host of other tangible and abstract goods and services are underfunded and undersupplied . It is no wonder that statistical measures of chronic disease , mental ill-health , antisocial activity and environmental deterioration are worsening !

@@121737750 <h> Han Kang We Do Not Part <p> A landscape of blackened trees that resemble thousands of huddled people . Nearby , burial mounds inundated by the sea . As she opens her 11th novel with this scene , the Korean writer Han Kang restages a recurring preoccupation : what do the living owe the dead ? <p> Han , who won the 2024 Nobel Prize for Literature , once told The White Review , " I believe that grief is something which situates the place/space of the dead within the living ; and that , through repeatedly revisiting that place , through our pained and silent embrace of it over the course of a whole life , life is , perhaps paradoxically , made possible . Han too had put that massacre of protesting civilians by government forces at the centre of a novel -- Human Acts ( 2014 ) . Kyungha 's psychological distress also evokes the shapeshifting Yeong-hye in Han 's The Vegetarian ( 2015 ) , who renounces meat and a suffocating marriage , preferring to become as harmless as a tree . <p> When We Do Not Part opens , Kyungha has been isolated in a Seoul apartment for two months after severing ties with many people in her life . As of last week , all 50 states have introduced right-to-repair legislation -- that is , laws designed to give people a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it to someone of their own choosing to have it repaired . <p> New York was the first state to sign right-to-repair legislation into law back in 2022 , followed by California , Minnesota , Oregon and Colorado . The final state to introduce legislation was Wisconsin . Not every state has passed legislation at this stage , but the fact that there 's no state in the US where it is n't being seriously discussed can be read as a victory for all of us owners of tech everywhere -- as well as for the planet . <p> The milestone " is n't just a legislative achievement -- it 's a cultural revolution , " Kyle Wiens , CEO of iFixit , an online community , advocacy group and parts retailer , told me over email . <p> I 've been covering consumer technology and climate change for years , and nowhere do the two topics intersect more closely than the problems caused by e-waste and the potential solutions created by accessible repair . The boom in right-to-repair legislation " reflects the growing concerns over the sheer volume of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Wood , chief analyst at CCS Insight . <p> The amount of electronic waste humans produce annually hit 62 million tons in 2022 , according to last year 's UN E-waste monitor -- that 's enough to fill a convoy of 40-ton trucks to stretch around the Equator . This increases pollution risks , as well as creating more emissions through the energy needed to produce replacement devices for the ones we discard . Both factors feed into the climate crisis , which is causing more extreme weather events across our increasingly hotter planet . <p> A small but mighty part of the solution is to ensure we 're maximizing the lifespan of any tech we do buy , keeping it out of landfill for as long as possible . Unfortunately , tech companies do n't always want us to do this -- it benefits their profit margins more if we buy replacements , rather than fix what we already have . <p> In the past decade or so , we 've seen tech companies including Apple and Samsung take important steps to improve the lifespan of devices by introducing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ repairs , at least to some degree . But that does n't mean they 're perfect -- far from it . <p> The planned obsolescence of technology tracks back to auto companies in the early 20th century , and the short lifecycle of expensive products is still a widespread problem today . Tech companies still want you to always be thinking about their next upgrade . <p> It 's easy to forget when you buy a new phone you 've been excited for , that some day in the not-too-distant future , it 's going to slow down to the point of becoming unusable , or simply break . <p> " Consumers have developed a love affair with gadgets but seldom consider what happens to them when they stop working , " said Wood over email . " Any efforts to make it easier to repair products and extend their lives has to be applauded . " <p> The driving force behind the slew of right-to-repair legislation popping up across the US -- and Europe as well -- is a movement formed of public interest groups , farmers , professionals @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has had an impact at a national , if not federal , scale . <p> " We 're witnessing the rebirth of a repair economy that values sustainability over planned obsolescence and empowers individuals over corporate gatekeepers , " said Wiens . <p> It 's not a partisan issue , he adds , aligning farmers in rural areas , who want to be able to fix their high-tech tractors , with urban tech nerds on the need to have true ownership over their tech . <p> " Each state that introduces legislation is another community recognizing that when you ' own ' something you ca n't understand , maintain , or modify , you 're not an owner at all -- just a perpetual renter with an upfront fee , " Wiens said . <p> And so , next time you 're replacing your giant but janky TV , or wondering whether the declining battery life of your smartwatch means you 'll have to replace it , just remember that you might have another option .
